newsitem.title: CHINA: China firms spurn B listings with eye on HK.
newsitem.headline: China firms spurn B listings with eye on HK.

text.p: China's stagnant B share stock markets are losing their appeal for domestic firms, many of which now see Hong Kong's more liquid bourse as a better way of raising foreign funds, analysts said on Friday.

Domestic currency A shares, with their higher price earnings ratios (P/Es), and the higher-profile Hong Kong-listed H shares were threatening to make China's foreign currency B share markets obsolete, they said.
"When a company wants to make an issue they will choose A shares first, then H shares and finally B shares," said an analyst with Crosby Securities in Shanghai.

Hesitancy to list on one of China's two B markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen is reflected in the number of new listings -- just six firms so far this year despite a quota of 33 new counters announced by Beijing in January.
"They will wait and see how the market is doing," the Crosby Securities analyst said.

In contrast, five mainland companies have listed in Hong Kong so far this year. Three more are scheduled to make their debuts in the 11 days before the British colony becomes a Chinese special administrative region, bringing the total to 37.
China now lists 92 B shares but their total capitalisation is only around $3 billion, prompting companies mulling a new listing to look to Hong Kong's more robust bourse, analysts said.
"Larger companies might be looking at Hong Kong or Singapore because the liquidity is much better than Shanghai or Shenzhen," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage.
"They are also able to make bigger listings in Hong Kong," said a broker.

Mainland companies have recently offered shares in Hong Kong with phenomenal success. Last month, Beijing Enterprises was nearly 1,300 times over-subscribed and this week's offer by First Tractor was nearly 300 times over-subscribed.

The July 1 return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule after 156 years of British rule would make mainland firms more eager to list in the territory as bullish sentiment powered the main Hang Seng Index to historic highs, said a second broker.
"The Hong Kong handover might have a positive impact on the market there, but companies will want to list H shares because of the liquidity," the analyst with the foreign brokerage said.
Hong Kong share prices staged a record-breaking rally on Friday, surging to an all-time high of 15,026.55 points before closing the morning session up 2.90 percent at 14,927.74.

But Beijing wants to be sure Hong Kong optimism does not spill over to the mainland exchanges out of fear that sharp rises before July 1 could set the markets up for a post-handover plunge, said a broker in Shanghai.
"The government doesn't want to give the feeling that the Hong Kong handover will help the B and A share markets, at least in the short term," the broker said.

While B share listings this year have been fully subscribed or over-subscribed, A counters are a better bet for companies because their P/Es are about double those for B shares, analysts said. H shares also offer slightly higher P/Es.
"There is still market interest in the B share IPOs despite the government crackdown on the B market," another analyst said.
Shanghai's A index soared from 973 points at the end of 1996 to a year high 1,578 points in early May, when official measures to cool the markets pulled it down to around 1,300 points.
The B index peaked at 99 points in May before returning to the low 80s, where it has since stagnated on flimsy turnover.
